title: S.O.H. Afriyie-Vidza: "Hearty Garlands"
summary: The poet, your lesson note's reading of the poem as a celebration of lasting love, another reading to check, and its themes and devices.

p: S.O.H. Afriyie-Vidza is a Ghanaian poet. His poem 'Hearty Garlands' is a set poem in the West African Literature in English syllabus. His voice is direct and sincere, and his subjects are personal feeling and life.

sections.h: The reading in your lesson note
p: Your note reads the poem as a simple, sincere love poem. The persona offers 'hearty garlands' (wreaths of flowers) to the person he loves. These garlands have been 'watered' not only by showers of grace (good times) but by faithful tears and sweat (hard times and effort). So the love that they stand for is a mature, tested love, strengthened by shared hardship.
Theme: enduring and resilient love. Mood and tone: celebratory and joyful; sincere, affectionate and grateful.

A summary on one Nigerian study site describes the poem as a celebration of long life and of what lies ahead, with a birthday of advanced age as its occasion. Both readings agree on the symbol of garlands as honour and celebration. Read the poem in your anthology and decide which details support each reading; in an examination, argue from the lines, and you can mention both.

Symbolism and metaphor: the garlands stand for love (or for honour and celebration); 'watered' makes love or life a plant that has been tended; tears and sweat stand for hardship and sacrifice. Diction: warm, positive words (hearty, faithful, beautiful, grace). Imagery: the sight and scent of flowers and the picture of watering.

sections.h: Model answer: what makes the garlands special?
p: The garlands are special because they are not given only in happy times. They are watered by tears and sweat as well as by blessing, so they show that the love or the life they celebrate has survived hard times. This makes the gift more valuable than a gift given in easy times.

title: Elizabeth L. A. Kamara: "New Tongue"
summary: The poet and the reading of the poem in your lesson note as the pain of taking on a foreign language and culture, with a caution to check against the text.

p: Elizabeth L. A. Kamara is a poet from Sierra Leone. 'New Tongue' is one of the African poems set for the West African syllabus. Your lesson note says her work often looks at identity, gender and the difficulty of living between cultures.

sections.h: The reading in your lesson note
p: The poem describes the painful and lonely experience of taking on a foreign language and culture. The 'new tongue' (probably English) tastes bitter. The persona has 'buried' her mother tongue, and the new language feels cold. Her own people cannot hear her, and her attempts to speak the new language slip and falter, so she feels like an impostor.

Themes: cultural alienation, loss of identity (language is part of who we are) and the pain of assimilation (fitting into a dominant culture is painful, not simple). Mood and tone: melancholy, isolated, frustrated.

I could not find a reliable independent summary of this poem to check your note against. Read the poem in your anthology and underline each word that supports the points above. If the poem seems to say something different, trust the poem.

Central metaphor: the 'new tongue' stands for the foreign language and the culture that comes with it. Imagery: taste (bitter), touch (cold) and sound (people who cannot hear her). Juxtaposition: the cold, bitter, slipping new tongue against the natural, warm, lost mother tongue that is only implied.

Many Nigerian students think and feel in Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa or Pidgin and write in English at school. The poem can help you to understand how language, belonging and identity are linked, and why it is important not to look down on mother tongues.

activity: Explain what the 'new tongue' is and how the persona feels about it. Pick one sensory image (taste, touch or sound) and explain its effect. Write a short paragraph on how language is linked to identity, with an example from your own life.

title: Comparing Poems: Tone and Word Choice
summary: How to compare the tone of two poems such as 'Hearty Garlands' and 'New Tongue', with a table and a model comparison.

p: To compare is to say how two poems are alike; to contrast is to say how they differ. For a good comparison, choose a few points (theme, tone, diction, imagery, structure) and discuss both poems under each, instead of describing one poem completely and then the other.

sections.h: Table: 'Hearty Garlands' and 'New Tongue' (using your lesson note)
p: Study the table.

head: Point
Hearty Garlands
New Tongue
rows: Enduring love (or life) that has survived hardship
Alienation and loss of identity through a foreign language
Warm, positive words (hearty, faithful, beautiful, grace)
Cold, negative words (bitter, cold, spat out, buried)

p: 'Hearty Garlands' and 'New Tongue' create very different feelings through word choice. The first poem is built from warm, positive words such as 'hearty', 'faithful' and 'beautiful', so the reader feels warmth and gratitude. The second uses words such as 'bitter' and 'cold' and speaks of burying the mother tongue, so the reader feels sadness and loneliness. In both poems the poet turns one image (garlands, tongue) into a symbol, but the first symbol brings people together, while the second shows a person cut off from her own people.

Paragraph 1: the tone of each poem, with a quotation for each. Paragraph 2: how word choice (diction) creates the tone, giving at least two words from each poem and their effects. End with one sentence that sums up the difference.

title: Maya Angelou: "Still I Rise"
summary: The poet, the situation and themes of 'Still I Rise', and its refrain, similes, metaphor, rhetorical questions and tone, with model answers.

p: Maya Angelou (1928 to 2014) was an American poet, memoirist and civil rights activist. Her writing is known for strong rhythms, accessible language and the themes of Black and female identity, resilience and empowerment.

'Still I Rise' is an anthem of defiance and triumph. The speaker, a Black woman, speaks directly to those who oppress her ('you'). She lists the ways in which they try to bring her down: to write her down in history with lies, to 'shoot' her with words, to 'kill' her with hatred. In spite of all this she declares that she will rise.

Resilience and perseverance (the core theme): she is trodden into the dirt but, like dust, she will rise. Empowerment: a declaration of self-worth, especially for women who face racism and sexism. Defiance: she is not a passive victim; she is sassy and challenges her oppressors. The unbeatable human spirit: a universal celebration of the power to overcome.
Direct address (apostrophe): speaking to 'You' makes the poem confrontational and strong.
Refrain: 'Still I rise' returns like a drumbeat and grows in power.

Simile: 'like dust' (common and looked down on, yet impossible to keep down); laughing as though she has gold mines in her backyard and walking as though oil wells pump in her living room (an inner wealth and confidence that the oppressors cannot see or take away).
Metaphor: she describes herself as a black ocean, wide and leaping (a vast, unstoppable power).
Rhetorical questions: she taunts her oppressors with questions that need no answer, such as whether her sassiness upsets them or whether they wanted to see her broken.
Tone: proud, defiant, sassy, joyous and triumphant.

sections.h: Model answer: the oil wells simile
p: The simile says that she walks as if she had oil wells pumping in her living room. Oil means great wealth, and 'in my living room' makes it personal and close. She walks with the confidence of a rich person even though she may not have money. It shows that her value and strength come from within and cannot be taken away by her oppressors.

An anthem is a song of pride and unity. The strong rhythm, the repeated refrain and the confident 'I' make the poem easy to chant and to perform, and it has been used to give courage to people facing injustice.

activity: Write two paragraphs on how Angelou uses rhetorical questions and similes to create a tone of defiance and empowerment. Say who the 'you' is. Explain what makes the poem an anthem.

title: Lord Byron: "She Walks in Beauty"
summary: The Romantic poet, the first stanza read slowly, the poem's themes of inner and outer beauty, and its devices and mood.

p: George Gordon, Lord Byron (1788 to 1824) was a leading poet of the British Romantic movement. The Romantics valued strong feeling, the beauty of nature and the inner life. Byron was a famous, passionate and rebellious figure, and his poems are known for their musical beauty and emotion.

This is a lyric poem (like a song) in praise of a woman whom the poet saw at a party. It does not describe only her face. It celebrates the harmony between her outer beauty (dark hair, bright eyes) and her inner beauty (peace, innocence and goodness).

'She walks in beauty, like the night / Of cloudless climes and starry skies; / And all that's best of dark and bright / Meet in her aspect and her eyes: / Thus mellow'd to that tender light / Which heaven to gaudy day denies.'

Meaning: her beauty is like a clear, starry night, not the harsh, showy light of day ('gaudy day'). In her, the best of dark and light meet, giving a soft, tender glow that the bright day cannot give.
Stanza 2: Her beauty is perfectly balanced: one shade more or one ray less would spoil her 'nameless grace'. Her black hair and calm face show the pure and dear thoughts in her mind.
Stanza 3: Her cheek, brow and winning smiles all tell of a life of goodness, a mind at peace with the world and a heart whose love is innocent.

The perfection of beauty. The harmony of inner and outer beauty (the central theme): her looks express her goodness. The power of innocence and purity: her gentle heart is the source of her calm and her smile.
Diction: elevated, graceful, soft words such as serenely, sweet, eloquent, peace, calm, innocent. Mood: admiration, reverence and calm.

Simile: 'like the night' is the main device. Juxtaposition: dark and bright; the gaudy day against the starry night. Personification: her face and smile are said to 'tell' and to be 'eloquent', as if they could speak. Alliteration and assonance (repeated sounds): 'cloudless climes', 'serenely sweet', which give a musical flow.

sections.h: Model answer: why night, not day?
p: The poet compares her beauty to night instead of day because night with stars is soft, calm and deep, while day is bright and showy. Her beauty is not loud but gentle and balanced, a harmony of light and dark. The comparison suggests a quiet, inward beauty.

title: Seamus Heaney: "Digging"
summary: The poet, the structure of memory in 'Digging', its central metaphor of the pen as a spade, its sound and smell imagery and its theme of heritage and craft.

p: Seamus Heaney (1939 to 2013) was an Irish poet who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1995. His poetry is rooted in the farmland of Ireland, his family and the past. He is known for 'earthy' language and for finding deep meaning in everyday objects and actions.

The poem begins in the present: the poet sits at his desk with a pen. He hears his father digging in the garden outside, and this brings a memory: his father digging potatoes twenty years before, and then a deeper memory of his grandfather cutting turf (peat). He admires their skill and strength. He realises that he has no spade to follow them, and he decides that he will use his pen as his tool and 'dig' into his roots, family history and memories.

The poem moves through time: present (the poet with his pen), recent past (his father), distant past (his grandfather), present again (the pen). The shape shows him digging into his own past. The tone is thoughtful, admiring and finally determined.
Central metaphor: the pen is the poet's spade; he writes that he will dig with it. The pen is also compared to a gun in the opening lines, a simile that makes it a tool with power.

Imagery: sound ('the clean rasping sound', 'the squelch and slap'), sight (the stooping rhythm, nicking and slicing) and smell (the cold smell of potato mould). Onomatopoeia: words that sound like what they mean, such as 'rasping', 'squelch' and 'slap'.

Family heritage, manual work and the craft of writing: Heaney cannot dig like his father and grandfather, but he honours their tradition by 'digging' with words. Writing is seen as work as serious as farming.

sections.h: Model answer: what does the pen stand for?
p: The pen stands for the poet's work as a writer, and it is compared to a spade, the tool of his father and grandfather. It shows that he will carry on the family tradition of hard work and 'digging' in a new way: to dig into memory and bring up the past in words.

title: Fleur Adcock: "The Telephone Call"
summary: The poet, and a summary of the poem as described by published guides: a surprise prize call, a twist and a satire on modern promises.

p: Fleur Adcock (born 1934) is a poet from New Zealand who spent most of her life in England. Her poems are often witty, conversational and ironic, and they notice the odd or absurd side of modern life.

sections.h: A note on your lesson note
p: Your lesson note stops after the poet's introduction and only calls the poem a study of 'modern alienation' with a 'sarcastic' tone in the revision week. It does not describe the poem. The summary below comes from published study guides, so read the poem in your anthology to check it.

The speaker answers a telephone call from a caller who says she has won a prize in a lottery: she is about to become a millionaire. Excited, she asks about the money. The caller replies that they do not deal in money; they deal in 'experiences', and the experience is her prize. The line then goes dead, and the speaker is left with her disappointment.

The poem has six stanzas of eight lines each and is written in free verse (no fixed rhyme or rhythm), which gives it a natural, conversational feel. The speaker is an ordinary person, which makes it easy for the reader to share her hopes and her disappointment.

Themes: expectation against reality; disappointment and fantasy (we dream of sudden wealth); a satire on empty promises and on the faceless way in which institutions talk to people. Tone: light and amused at first, then sharply ironic and sarcastic. Devices: irony (the 'prize' is not what she wanted), the shock of the final twist, and the conversational tone that makes the reader feel part of the call.

sections.h: Model answer: how does the poem use irony?
p: The irony lies in the gap between the speaker's expectation of a fortune and the caller's offer of an 'experience'. The word 'prize' leads us to expect riches, but the final reply turns out to be nothing of value. The poet uses this to mock how advertisers and organisations promise much and give little.

sections.h: How to answer a poetry question
p: 1. Read the question carefully and underline the key words (theme, tone, device). 2. Plan three points. 3. For each point, make a statement, quote briefly, and explain the effect. 4. Write in clear paragraphs. 5. Finish with a sentence that answers the question again.

Compare 'Once Upon a Time' with 'Not My Business': which one criticises society more directly, and how? Which poem do you find most moving, and why? Compare the tone of 'Still I Rise' with that of 'New Tongue'. How do Okara and Osundare use simple language to make strong points? How do Angelou and Heaney use a central comparison to carry their meaning?

Re-read each poem aloud. Write one sentence for each stanza. Learn two short quotations and one device for each poem. Practise paragraphs with a friend and mark each other's work. Do a past paper in exam time.
